description: NEXUS//04 is an interactive space exploration game where players design a spacecraft, launch missions to four real destinations—the asteroid Apophis, the Moon, Earth’s atmosphere, and Mars—and make tough choices about power, fuel, instruments, and communications. Inspired by real NASA missions and research, the game shows how those choices affect a spacecraft’s survival and the science it can bring home.
summary:
NEXUS//04 is a free browser game where you design, launch and fly your own science mission. Pick one of four targets modelled on real NASA missions: asteroid Apophis (OSIRIS-APEX), the Moon’s coldest craters (LRO), Earth’s atmosphere (Terra, Aqua and Aura) or Jezero crater on Mars (MRO). Build the spacecraft inside a budget by choosing instruments, solar arrays, battery, radio, recorder, orbit and rocket. Every choice changes mass, power, propellant and how much data can reach Earth.

You then fly it orbit by orbit. The battery drains in eclipse, the recorder fills between contacts, and faults force quick decisions. A debrief shows how much science came home and why. The game runs real physics (Kepler orbits, eclipse geometry, the rocket equation, energy budgets) and every value is labelled NASA fact, team research or game value, with its source. It addresses the challenge by turning the hidden trade-offs of mission design into something anyone can try, learn from and replay, with no install or login.
details:
What it does

Real space missions are a chain of trade-offs: power against mass, data against downlink, ambition against budget and propellant. Most people only ever see the pictures that come back. NEXUS//04 hands those decisions to the player and shows exactly how each one shapes the result.

How it works

Every mission follows five stages.

1. Brief: VEGA, the flight director, sets the target and what success means. ASTRA studies asteroid Apophis as Earth's gravity pulls on it during its close pass on 13 April 2029. LUNARIS reads permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's south pole. HALO watches aerosols, ozone and clouds from a 705 km sun-synchronous orbit. JEZERO ECHO reads the ancient lake in Jezero crater from Mars orbit.

2. Build: choose from 17 instruments with real heritage (for example LROC, LOLA and Diviner from LRO; MODIS, OMI, AIRS and MLS from Terra, Aqua and Aura; CTX, HiRISE and CRISM from MRO), then size the solar arrays, battery, radio, recorder, orbit, propellant and rocket. Six go/no-go checks (mass, budget, propellant, eclipse power, peak power, science coverage) explain anything that will not work before launch.

3. Launch: every station votes go or no-go, then a full 3D launch with live telemetry.

4. Operate: the mission runs orbit by orbit with eclipses, target passes and ground contact windows. The player manages instruments, battery and recorder, and handles faults on harder levels.

5. Debrief: a grade, the science returned in gigabits, the physics behind every loss, and a better build to try next.

Three levels (Cadet, Flight, Commander) suit first-time players and people who want a real engineering puzzle.

The physics is real

Orbital period comes from Kepler's law, time in shadow from the planet's radius, propellant from the rocket equation, and power from array output, derating and battery efficiency. Example from the game: HALO at 705 km has a 98.7 minute orbit with 35.2 minutes in Earth's shadow, so the spacecraft needs about 120 Wh to survive each eclipse. The small battery fails; the large one passes. Every value is labelled as published (NASA or JPL), team (from our four research documents) or conceptual (chosen for gameplay), and links to its source.

Beyond the game

The Cosmic Explorer and Nova's Quests carry the learning outward: six interactive story chapters (nebulae, star life, planet formation, black holes, gravitational lensing and a tour across cosmic scales) with 142 parts and 426 stars to earn. Mission Control, a 3D Explore view of each world, a Satellite Hangar and a 3D Mission Briefing complete the site.

Benefits and impact

It is free, needs no install or login, and runs in any modern browser on phones and school laptops. It is built for students and curious beginners, and for teachers who want every number traceable to a source. Players learn why engineers argue about grams, watts and megabits by failing a mission and reading why.

Creativity and team factors

Instead of reading about mission design, players learn by flying and failing. We focused on scientific honesty (labelled values, sources one click away), accessibility (works on low-end devices, no account), fairness (every mission and level was tested so it can be won) and clarity for beginners.

Tools, languages and software

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules); three.js and WebGL shaders for 3D; Web Audio; ffmpeg for video; Playwright for automated testing; GitHub and GitHub Pages for code and hosting.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence) tools

The research is our team's own work: the four mission concepts, the science facts, instrument choices, component values and every source were found, read and checked by us. We used AI tools to generate the website and game code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript and shaders), the 3D scenes and visual effects, the Cosmic Explorer films and parts of the presentation text. The team reviewed, tested and edited all of it and checked every fact against its source. AI-generated visuals carry a visible "AI-generated visuals" watermark on every page, inside every film and on every screenshot in our demo. AI generation of the code is stated in the repository README and in a disclosure meta tag on each page. No NASA logos, flags or mission insignia are used.

Team

Sneha (ASTRA research, opening experience and navigation), Karishma (LUNARIS research, integration and quality checks), Kshitij (HALO research, lead website developer, mission worlds and spacecraft), Anttariksha (JEZERO ECHO research, mission control and challenges).
